Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 11 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 502 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Every June, students leave school with a packet in hand, and every August many of them return with that packet finished in a rushed weekend. Summer projects are meant to keep minds active over the break, but the way they are designed decides whether they do. I believe summer projects should be student-designed, with teachers setting clear guidelines and checkpoints. When students choose what they study, they work harder, learn more deeply, and practice skills that a worksheet cannot teach.

The first reason is motivation. Summer is the one stretch of the year when students have real freedom, and a project that ignores their interests feels like a punishment for having a vacation. A teacher-designed assignment, such as reading three assigned novels and answering questions about each, usually gets done at the last minute because nobody cares about it. Compare that to a student who loves baseball and decides to track batting averages all summer, build graphs, and figure out which players improved. That student is doing statistics without being forced to, and is likely to keep going long after the minimum is met. Interest is the fuel that makes summer learning happen at all.

The second reason is that designing a project is itself a valuable skill. In school, teachers usually hand students the question, the materials, and the deadline. Adults, however, rarely get such clear instructions. A student who has to pick a topic, plan the steps, find resources, and manage time over ten weeks is practicing exactly the independence that college and jobs demand. My cousin, for example, decided one summer to learn how to repair old bicycles. She had to watch tutorials, buy parts on a budget, and keep notes on what failed. By September she had fixed four bikes and sold two, and she had learned more about planning than any packet could have taught her.

Third, student-designed projects respect the fact that students are different. A single teacher-designed project assumes that everyone has the same interests, the same resources, and the same summer schedule. One student might spend July caring for younger siblings, while another travels or works a part-time job. Letting students design their own projects allows each of them to find something that fits their real lives, whether that is writing a family history, starting a garden, or coding a simple game.

Critics argue that students left on their own will choose easy projects or do nothing at all. This concern is fair, but it is a reason for structure, not for taking away choice. Teachers can require a short proposal before school ends, set a few standards for effort and evidence, and ask for a brief presentation in the fall. That way students keep ownership while teachers keep accountability.

Summer projects exist to keep students learning, not just to keep them busy. When students design their own work with a teacher's guidance, they care about it, grow as independent thinkers, and come back in the fall with something they are proud to share.
